title: The Alhambra
hookLine: the red palace of Granada, walls covered with the words, no victor but Allah

lines: LACE THAT TURNS OUT TO BE WRITING.
cards: Stand in a courtyard in Granada and look closely at the wall. What looks like lace from a few steps back turns out, up close, to be writing: Arabic letters carved into plaster, woven through vines and stars.
Some of it is the Qur'an. Some is poetry, praising the very room you're standing in. And again and again, one short sentence, small enough to fit in a corner and patient enough to fill a palace.
Wa la ghaliba illa Allah. There is no victor but God.

teach.h: THE RED PALACE ON THE HILL.
teach.b: The Alhambra sits on a hill above Granada. Its name is said to mean the red one, for the color of its walls. It was the palace of the Nasrid rulers of Granada.
By then their map had shrunk: the Christian kingdoms had taken city after city, and Granada was what remained. That makes the motto worth hearing twice.

People tell a story about it. The dynasty's founder came home from a battle, and the crowd hailed him as the victor. His answer, so the story goes, was the sentence that would cover his family's palace: no victor but God.
Nobody can confirm the scene, but the sentence is carved there for anyone to read. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an word for word, but it leans on one.

In Pickthall's translation: "Victory cometh only from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." A ruler writing that on his own walls says something odd for a ruler: the win is not mine; the throne answers to someone else.
The writing doesn't sit on top of the decoration; it is the decoration. Letters climb, interlace, turn into borders. Geometry repeats without ending.
Some poems speak in the room's own voice, as if the building were talking. A palace that keeps reminding its owners who owns it.

how: Visitors to the Alhambra, Muslim and not, read the motto 'no victor but God' carved throughout its walls; Muslims often say that victory comes only from God, echoing the Qur'an.

games.q: you're the founder of a dynasty, home from battle. the crowd is shouting that you are the victor. what do you say?
o: nothing; you wave and go inside.
games.why: in the story people tell, he answers: no victor but God. his family then carved that sentence across their palace walls.

practice: Picture a wall where one sentence is carved over and over among leaves and stars, until your eye stops seeing the pattern and starts reading it.
Then bring to mind something you've won lately, a deadline met, an argument settled, a good day, and hold it lightly beside the sentence: no victor but God.
If you pray, let those words rest on your breath; if you don't, notice how it feels to hold a win more loosely.
